Tirzah
TUR-zah
proper noun
Hebrew Tirtsah, “delight” or “pleasantness,” a Canaanite royal city that became the early capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria.

See also: Tirzah

Biblical Definition

Tirzah was a city of beauty and of blood. Its name means delight, and Solomon set it beside Jerusalem as the very figure of loveliness: “Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners” (Son 6:4). Yet this fair city became the seat of apostate kings. To Tirzah Jeroboam’s wife came in vain to save her dying son: “And Jeroboam’s wife arose, and departed, and came to Tirzah: and when she came to the threshold of the door, the child died” (1Ki 14:17). There Baasha reigned, and there Elah his son after him — “began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah” (1Ki 16:8) — until Zimri murdered him and, besieged, “burnt the king’s house over him with fire, and died” (1Ki 16:18). Omri would soon abandon Tirzah for Samaria. So the delight of the north became a byword for treachery and short-lived crowns. The lesson is stern: outward beauty and a pleasant name cannot cover a throne built on idolatry. The city comely as Jerusalem was not comely in the sight of God, for its kings walked in the sin of Jeroboam. Loveliness without holiness is a whited sepulchre.

Webster 1828 Definition

The early capital of the northern kingdom (1Ki 16:8), a city whose name means “delight” (Son 6:4) yet became a seat of apostate, blood-stained kings.

TIRZAH, a Canaanite royal city, later the first capital of Israel before Omri built Samaria.

Its name signifies “delight” or “pleasantness”; Solomon likened his beloved to it (Son 6:4).

Jeroboam dwelt there; his child died at its threshold (1Ki 14:17).

Baasha and Elah reigned there until Zimri’s treachery and self-inflicted fire (1Ki 16:18).

A witness that a fair name cannot cover a throne of idolatry.

Key Scripture

Son 6:4 — "Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners."

1Ki 14:17 — "And Jeroboam's wife arose, and departed, and came to Tirzah: and when she came to the threshold of the door, the child died;"

1Ki 16:8 — "began Elah the son of Baasha to reign over Israel in Tirzah, two years."

1Ki 16:18 — "he went into the palace of the king's house, and burnt the king's house over him with fire, and died,"

Modern Corruption

The delightful early capital of the north; the entry recovers that outward beauty and a fair name cannot sanctify a throne built on idolatry.

expand to see more

Tirzah’s corruption is the ancient confusion of beauty with goodness. A city named delight, comely as Jerusalem, was nonetheless the seat of Jeroboam’s calves and of murdering kings. The eye admired what the heart of God abhorred. The perennial temptation is to reckon a thing holy because it is lovely, or true because it is admired.

The modern form of the error prizes the aesthetic and the appealing above the holy: what pleases the eye and the taste is called good, and beauty is made its own justification. But Tirzah teaches that a fair name and a comely face may crown an idolatrous throne. The Lord looks not on the outward appearance but on the heart (1Sa 16:7). Loveliness severed from obedience is the whited sepulchre; only holiness makes a city truly comely before God.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Tirtsah, “delight,” a royal city and the first capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria.

expand to see more

Tirzah — Hebrew Tirtsah, “delight, pleasantness.”

A Canaanite royal city conquered under Joshua.

The first capital of the northern kingdom before Omri built Samaria.

Home to Jeroboam, Baasha, Elah, and the usurper Zimri.

Set beside Jerusalem as an emblem of beauty in the Song (Son 6:4).

Usage

"Solomon likened his beloved to Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem."

"Elah drank himself drunk in Tirzah while Zimri conspired against him."

"Tirzah preaches that a delightful name cannot sanctify an idolatrous crown."
